claims: Immunization prevents millions of deaths annually.
Vaccines introduce deactivated or weakened parts of a virus or bacteria (antigens) into the body.
Vaccines cause an imitation infection that does not cause disease.
Vaccines teach the immune system to create T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes (memory cells).
Memory cells allow for a rapid response upon future exposure.
Active immunization teaches the body to produce its own antibodies.
Types of active immunization include inactivated vaccines, live-attenuated vaccines, messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, and subunit/conjugate vaccines.
Passive immunization provides temporary protection by introducing antibodies directly (e.g., immunoglobulin) from another human or animal source.
Routine pediatric vaccinations include DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis), MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), Varicella (chickenpox), Hib, Pneumococcal, and Polio.
Adolescents and adults vaccinations include HPV (human papillomavirus), COVID-19, Influenza, and Tdap.
Common vaccine side effects include fever, pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site.
Serious side effects of vaccines are rare.
